system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2198-02-15 19:53:00 to 2198-02-17 14:56:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted with sepsis likely originating from a urinary source, given his history of nephrolithiasis and presenting symptoms of fever, flank pain, and urinary symptoms. He was tachycardic and febrile on arrival, with leukocytosis and elevated lactate, consistent with severe sepsis. Imaging showed a nonobstructing left staghorn calculus and mild perinephric fat stranding, suggesting pyelonephritis. He received IV vancomycin and cefepime initially, then transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin after Klebsiella pneumoniae was identified. His course was complicated by an elevated INR of 4.0 on admission, which was managed by holding warfarin temporarily and later reducing the dose to 4 mg daily. He developed transient acute kidney injury after restarting torsemide 50 mg daily, leading to volume depletion; this was corrected by switching to PRN low-dose torsemide based on weight changes. He improved clinically, became afebrile, and was discharged home on oral antibiotics and adjusted anticoagulation with follow-up planned for urology and INR monitoring.

procedures.long_title: Transurethral removal of obstruction from ureter and renal pelvis

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of the urology team. You were brought in after your procedure today because you had some chills and a slight fever in recovery. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit shaky still, and my back pain is better, but I feel warm. Is that normal after the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The back pain improving is a good sign. The chills and low-grade fever are why we’re keeping you overnight. We want to make sure there’s no infection from the stone or the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a stent before and got sepsis. I’m worried it’s happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re being cautious. You have a history of urosepsis, so we started you on IV fluids and antibiotics just in case. We’ve drawn blood and urine cultures to check for bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more surgery? The stone was big, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a 1.3 cm stone at the ureteropelvic junction. Today’s procedure went well—your surgeon used a laser to break it up and placed a new stent to keep the ureter open. Most of the stone was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not done with passing stones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might pass small fragments over the next few weeks. The stent can cause urgency, frequency, and some blood in the urine—that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stent—when does that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow up with Dr. Lee in clinic to have it removed. It’s very important you keep that appointment—stents can cause infections if left in too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my heart? I have a mechanical valve and take warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted cardiology. You’re on warfarin, so we held it briefly around the surgery. You can restart tonight. Your INR will need checking soon to adjust the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My dose has changed before. Will it change again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll let your anticoagulation clinic guide that. They’ll check your INR and adjust to keep it between 2.5 and 3.5, which is safe for your valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Your labs from last night show your white blood cell count was high at 17.7, but it’s coming down today to 5.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was elevated, which is why we started antibiotics. But you haven’t had a real fever, and your repeat labs look much better. The urine culture came back with no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria? So I’m not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No growth in the urine, and your blood cultures are still pending, but you’re clinically improving. We think the chills were a reaction, not full sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my kidneys? Last time I was in, my creatinine went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 1.5 yesterday but is back to 1.2 today. That’s normal for you. We’ve been giving IV fluids, and you’re urinating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m on torsemide—should I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart your 30 mg daily. We’ll monitor your weight and electrolytes. Your potassium is a bit low, so keep taking your Klor-Con three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blood cultures are back—no growth. That’s excellent news. We’re stopping the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on IV meds anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll switch to oral antibiotics—Bactrim twice a day for seven days—to be safe. Also, phenazopyridine for three days to help with bladder irritation from the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That orange urine I heard about—that’s from the phenazopyridine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Don’t worry if your urine turns orange—it’s harmless and just helps numb the bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve been using the oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can keep using it as needed, but try to switch to acetaminophen when possible. Also, take Colace daily to prevent constipation from the narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting more than 10 pounds, no vigorous activity for four weeks. Drink plenty of fluids—about 2 liters a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds? I take glyburide and metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume both. Your blood sugar was 105 today—well controlled. Keep monitoring at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’ve done well. You’re afebrile, eating and walking normally, and labs are stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the Bactrim and phenazopyridine as prescribed. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds. And follow up with urology to remove the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call the clinic today to schedule. Anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home meds, including warfarin. Contact your anticoagulation clinic for INR check. And call your cardiologist to review your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, drink fluids, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted following a right ureteroscopy, laser lithotripsy, and double-J stent placement for a 1.3 cm obstructing ureteral stone. He developed rigors and a low-grade fever in the PACU, prompting admission for sepsis workup. He was hydrated with IV fluids and started on empiric antibiotics. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth, white count normalized, and he remained afebrile. His cardiac enzymes were negative, and he tolerated oral intake and ambulation. He was discharged on oral sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and phenazopyridine, with instructions to follow up for stent removal and INR monitoring. His chronic conditions, including heart failure, diabetes, and anticoagulation, were managed without complication.
